chapter_title: Chương 73: 0073 [Tâm Bão Dư Luận, Đầu Sóng Ngọn Gió]

segments.title: Chương 73: 0073 [Tâm Bão Dư Luận, Đầu Sóng Ngọn Gió]
segments.content:
By the second semester of senior year, time suddenly became tight. Even the day students had no time to go home for meals.

For instance, school let out at 12:00 PM, and the lunchtime self-study session started at 12:30 PM.

There was only half an hour to eat, which included time for queuing, as well as running back and forth between the classroom and the cafeteria. The actual time spent eating was usually no more than fifteen minutes.

The real impressive characters could finish the battle in two minutes, swallowing their food without even chewing.

Bian Guanyue was having a hard time adapting!

It was during the lunchtime self-study session when the head teacher, Liu Shuying, called out, "Chen Guiliang, come out for a moment."

Chen Guiliang put down his test paper and walked out.

Liu Shuying said, "A reporter from the Longdu Daily is here. Come with me to the principal's office."

Longdu City currently had only this one newspaper; the district and county papers had already ceased publication, and an evening paper had not yet been launched.

"Student Chen Guiliang is here!"

Principal Yan stood up with a broad smile, appearing exceptionally amiable and approachable.

This was not an act. He was always like this and had never been seen to lose his temper.

His achievements last year were remarkable: producing the provincial top scorer in the science stream, successfully upgrading the school to a provincial key high school, and hosting a centennial celebration that brought back many famous alumni. He also used Guo Xiao Si to boost the school's fame, and the youth environmental protection innovation project also ranked first in the country.

In another two years, he was set to become a government official.

"Hello, Principal."

"These two are Reporter Yuan and Reporter Xiong."

"Hello, Reporter Yuan. Hello, Reporter Xiong."

Reporter Yuan was in his thirties, a print journalist. Reporter Xiong was in his forties, a photojournalist.

They came for the interview purely as a formality, and to collect a travel stipend of one or two hundred yuan. It would have been fine if the school didn't give them money, they wouldn't have said anything, but giving it naturally fostered a more harmonious relationship.

They were also here to take a photo of Chen Guiliang.

As for the content of the report, the school had already written a draft. The reporters just had to take it back and revise it a little.

During the actual interview, whatever Chen Guiliang said, it was basically impossible for it to be published, unless it was particularly beneficial to the school's image.

This was how small-city daily papers operated; harmony was the priority.

So, the details of the interview are not worth mentioning, as it was all just politically correct nonsense.

After taking the photos and collecting their money, the two reporters took off. They had other interview assignments.

As the reporters and the head teacher were leaving together, Principal Yan called Chen Guiliang to a halt and said, like a family elder, "The second semester of senior year is a heavy workload. Are you adjusting well?"

"The head teacher and all the subject teachers are very good," Chen Guiliang said, seemingly answering a different question.

Principal Yan praised, "Compared to your sophomore year, you've matured a lot."

Chen Guiliang said, "People always go through a process of growth."

Principal Yan was even more pleased. "The personal materials needed for the independent recruitment exam have been prepared for you by the school. Your Teacher Liu will give them to you this afternoon. Have you decided which university you want to attend?"

"I'm still waiting for news from Tsinghua and Peking. They need to hold a meeting to discuss it," Chen Guiliang said.

Principal Yan said, "Some media outlets are coming at the end of the month. A normal interview might not be very effective. But a press conference seems like making a mountain out of a molehill. Do you have any ideas on how you can showcase your literary talent and proficiency in classical Chinese?"

Chen Guiliang thought carefully for a moment. "How about I give a language class in the multimedia classroom? It would showcase the school's software and hardware, and also highlight my own classical Chinese skills."

"How would you teach the class?" Principal Yan was intrigued.

Chen Guiliang said, "Teachers and students can voluntarily come to the multimedia classroom to listen, and the reporters can also sit in the audience. I'll focus on the errors in the language textbook. That would definitely be a hot topic, and the reporters would find it novel."

Principal Yan was surprised. "There are errors in the language textbook?"

Chen Guiliang nodded and said, "There's a mistaken annotation in the 'Preface to the Pavilion of Prince Teng,' which causes students to misunderstand the entire text."

Principal Yan said, "Explain it to me in detail."

Was the opportunity to boost Chen Guiliang's public profile that article from the Xihua Metropolis Daily?

Not entirely.

The real opportunity came from reforms in the Gaokao and university admissions!

Official media had already grasped the spirit of the higher-ups and began raising the topic of educational fairness since the second half of last year.

Even that article in Southern Weekly was riding this wave.

After the Spring Festival, the related public discourse entered its second phase, successively exposing old cases of Gaokao and admissions fraud.

Ms. Chai, who in the future would be reviled by all, was still a good reporter pleading for the people. In the CCTV program "News Investigation," she exposed how a top music conservatory had engaged in shady dealings during its recent arts entrance exam.

Candidates with major mistakes were ranked high, while students with excellent performances faced elimination.

The program's broadcast set off a huge wave. More instances of examination and admissions irregularities were exposed by television stations and newspapers!

Even the New Concept Composition Competition was pushed into the limelight.

Han Han's make-up exam was dug up and rehashed, with fingers pointing directly at the first and second-generation winners who had been granted direct admission.

At this very moment, Southern Weekly published another article, discussing the rationality of top universities vying for Chen Guiliang. That is, if a student writes well, are they truly qualified to be sought after for special admission?

Chen Guiliang instantly became the focus of public opinion!

The war of words began.

Southern Metropolis Daily picked up the baton, playing its old trick: publishing letters from readers.

From the Republican era to the present day, these so-called reader letters might be genuine when a discussion heats up, but at the beginning, they were always self-directed performances.

First, impersonate a reader and write a letter of opposition. Then, impersonate another reader and write a letter of support. They would even deliberately leave logical loopholes to attract more real readers to write in with rebuttals.

The two publications, Southern Metropolis and Southern Weekly, were putting on a show for a very simple purpose.

Just six words: attract attention, boost sales!

As for what conclusion the debate might reach in the end, they wouldn't consider it, nor could they be bothered to care.

"As a parent of a high school senior, I believe that granting special admission for a New Concept first-prize winner is inappropriate and does not conform to the principles of openness, fairness, and justice..."

"First, let's talk about openness. In the first New Concept Composition Competition, they actually allowed a separate make-up exam, and the proctor came up with the topic on the spot. Is it possible there was prior collusion? Could it be that someone ghostwrote it, and the person just memorized it for the make-up exam? There are too many opportunities for backdoor dealings. How can this be convincing?"

"Next, fairness. Ordinary students study hard for years, fighting their way across a single-plank bridge with thousands of others. The Gaokao can change a person's life. On what grounds can someone get a helicopter ride across the river just by writing an essay? Is this fair to the countless students?"

"Finally, justice. For science competitions, the process and results are objective. But awarding prizes in a writing competition is a purely subjective act. What justice is there to speak of? You say this essay is well-written, but I could say it's worse than a primary schooler's composition! If a certain contestant knows a judge personally, would the judge do them a favor and give a high score?"

"Due to public outcry, New Concept winners haven't been granted direct admission for three years. On what grounds can Chen Guiliang be specially admitted by Tsinghua and Peking this year?"

This so-called "reader's letter," riding on the hottest topic of admissions fairness, quickly sparked a heated debate nationwide.

A large number of genuine reader letters poured in, calling for the cancellation of special admissions for liberal arts competitions.

Letters supporting Chen Guiliang also quickly appeared, listing talented individuals with lopsided skills since the late Qing Dynasty. For example, a certain master who scored zero on all other exams but was outstanding in one or two subjects, was ultimately admitted to a prestigious university, and went on to make great contributions to the nation.

At the same time, they criticized the Gaokao system as unreasonable, causing many students with special talents to lose the opportunity to pursue higher education.

Back and forth they went, with sharp words and witty retorts. The war of words had begun.

When other media outlets saw this, they thought, why should you be the only one boosting sales? We want a piece of the pie too!

Consequently, more and more media outlets joined the discussion on this topic.

Some newspapers, unprepared, directly quoted the article from Xihua Metropolis Daily and published both of Chen Guiliang's poems in full. They didn't discuss admissions fairness, but instead focused their reports on Chen Guiliang himself and his writings.

"A Journey to Yinghai" and "Reply to Editor Dong of <Pen Club>" finally transitioned from being a concern of the internet and a few media outlets to something that ordinary people came to spectate and judge.

Many writers and literary critics also jumped in, taking the opportunity to boost their own presence.

Some praised his work effusively, while others cursed it as complete nonsense.

There were even newspapers that used Chen Guiliang to discuss left-behind children and rural education.

It was utter pandemonium.

Given the loud chorus of criticism, Tsinghua and Peking Universities held fiercely contentious meetings to debate whether to lower the score requirement for Chen Guiliang's special admission.

This wave of public opinion would not end anytime soon; its intensity would continue to rise.

This was because reform of the Gaokao and admissions was imperative, and officials had been fanning the flames from behind the scenes. In another two months, even the Ministry of Education itself would step in, announcing four major cases of examination fraud at once.

It wasn't just the Gaokao, but also the College English Test Band 4. A well-known university had its qualification as a CET-4 test center directly revoked.

More than one or two people went to jail, charged with intentionally leaking state secrets!

Even up to this year's Gaokao, there were still quite a few people who defied the risks. And during the period for filling out college applications, they would be ferreted out one by one, dealt with severely, and publicized as a warning to others.

Chen Guiliang had been unwittingly swept into the tide of the times.

Regardless, Chen Guiliang became nationally famous, and was generally recognized as a "talented scholar" and an "aspirational youth."

But many people also insisted that even a talented scholar should not be given special admission, as it was a matter of principle.

The Mengya magazine office was at its wit's end, because prestigious universities were calling one after another to say they would no longer offer reduced-score admission spots for New Concept winners next year. They had to lie low for a while.

Principal Yan of No. 2 High School, however, was very happy. Media outlets that had previously been unwilling to come had all changed their minds.

Some even showed up uninvited.

A date was set, and more than fifty media outlets descended upon the school
